entry.title: Extending a visible isotopy of an unknotted circle in $\mathbb R^3$
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $S^1\subseteq\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the unit circle with inclusion map $f_0$, and let $f_1:S^1\to\mathbb R^3$ be a round circle of radius $\lambda>0$ centred at $c\in\mathbb R^3$, written as the affine image $f_1(x)=c+\lambda Qf_0(x)$ of $f_0$ for some $Q\in SO(3)$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ and $H_1\circ f_0=f_1$: every round circle is carried to every other by an ambient isotopy supported in any prescribed open neighbourhood of the entire isotopy image $F(S^1\times I)$ constructed below. The example exhibits the hypothesis check of [[thm-isotopy-extension]] in the simplest case ($M=S^1$ compact, $N=\mathbb R^3$ without boundary, no boundary stratum, no properness issue) and shows that the visible motion of a round circle is always realisable ambiently.
entry.strategy: Write $f_1=c+\lambda Q f_0$ with $Q\in SO(3)$; if the given parametrisation of the target circle is a negatively oriented affine image, precompose with the rotation of $S^1$ by $\pi$, which is itself an isotopy of the source through diffeomorphisms and hence changes $f_1$ by an isotopy of embeddings, reducing to the displayed case. Choose the explicit smooth path $Q_t$ in $SO(3)$ from $Q_0=\mathrm{id}$ to $Q_1=Q$ given by rotating about the axis of $Q$ through the angle $t\theta$, where $\theta$ is the rotation angle of $Q$, and put $F_t(x):=t\,c+((1-t)+t\lambda)Q_tf_0(x)$. Each $F_t$ is the restriction of an invertible affine map (a rotation, a homothety with positive factor and a translation), hence an embedding of $S^1$, and $F$ is smooth on $S^1\times I$ with $F_0=f_0$ and $F_1=f_1$. Since the source is compact, clause 4 of [[thm-isotopy-extension]] applies and produces the required compactly supported ambient isotopy, supported in any prescribed neighbourhood of the track $F(S^1\times I)$. Countable choice is inherited from the isotopy extension theorem.

entry.title: Compact isotopic submanifolds have isomorphic normal bundles and diffeomorphic complements
entry.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold and let $f_0,f_1:M	o N$ be isotopic embeddings with normal bundles $
u_0=f_0^*TN/TM$ and $
u_1=f_1^*TN/TM$ ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]). Then $
u_0\cong
u_1$ as smooth vector bundles over $M$ and $N\setminus f_0(M)\cong N\setminus f_1(M)$; under AC every characteristic class defined on these normal bundles agrees (for orientation-dependent classes, use orientations transported by the displayed bundle isomorphism) and the complements are diffeomorphic. The example verifies the two embedding invariants supplied by isotopy: the ambient diffeomorphism of [[cor-isotopic-embeddings-have-diffeomorphic-complements]] intertwines the normal bundles, and [[thm-isotopy-extension]] is the source of that diffeomorphism. (The converse fails: trivial normal bundles do not force isotopy, as the reflected-sphere counterexample on this page shows.)
entry.strategy: Let $H$ be the ambient isotopy of [[thm-isotopy-extension]] with $H_t\circ f_0=F_t$ and $H\circ f_0=f_1$. Its differential restricts to a bundle isomorphism $TN|_{f_0(M)}\to TN|_{f_1(M)}$ covering $f_1\circ f_0^{-1}$; on the level of $M$ it induces a bundle map $\nu_0\to\nu_1$ over the identity of $M$ because the tangent summand $TM$ is carried to $TM$ by the chain rule $dH\circ df_0=df_1$. A bundle map that is an isomorphism on each fibre is a bundle isomorphism, so characteristic classes agree. The complement statement is [[cor-isotopic-embeddings-have-diffeomorphic-complements]]. The parenthetical failure of the converse is the content of the reflected-sphere counterexample on this page. Countable choice is inherited.

entry.title: A reflected sphere embedding is regularly homotopic but not isotopic to the standard one
entry.strategy: Clause 1: both maps are immersions, and [[thm-smale-classification-of-sphere-immersions-in-euclidean-space]], clause 3, records that for $m=2,n=3$ all immersions $S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ are regularly homotopic because $\pi_2(SO(3))=0$; the formal-data computation is the one of the DT-26 pair, consumed here through its classification theorem ([[cor-regular-homotopy-classes-of-immersions-are-formal-homotopy-classes]]). entry.title: The double point dimension count for surfaces in four- and five-space
entry.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M^2$ be a closed connected surface ($m=2$). Then:

1. for a self-transverse immersion $f:M^2\looparrowright\mathbb R^4$ the expected dimension is $2m-n=0$: the double point locus is a closed $0$-dimensional submanifold of $M\times M\setminus\Delta_M$, the double point set is finite, and the selected branch pairs are isolated and transverse; several pairs may initially have the same collision image;
2. for a self-transverse immersion $f:M^2\looparrowright\mathbb R^5$ the expected dimension is $-1<0$: the double point locus is empty, so $f$ is an injective immersion, and since $M$ is closed $f$ is an embedding.

The example shows why dimension four is the critical case for surfaces: it is exactly there that the double points are isolated rather than absent, so that the algebraic branch-pair count can be nonzero; the $m\ge3$ disjunction theorem does not cover this surface-in-four-space case. In five-space the configuration space argument already forbids double points.
entry.strategy: Both clauses are the dimension count [[lem-double-point-locus-has-expected-dimension-two-m-minus-n]] specialised to $m=2$: the locus is a closed embedded submanifold of dimension $2m-n$ when that is nonnegative, and empty when it is negative. For clause 1, local injectivity of the immersion ([[cor-every-immersion-is-locally-an-embedding]]) together with compactness of $M$ gives a neighbourhood of the diagonal in $M\times M$ containing no double point pair, so $\Delta_2(f)$ is a closed subset of the compact complement of that neighbourhood; being 0-dimensional it is discrete and compact, hence finite, and so is its image $\Sigma(f)$. For clause 2, emptiness of the double point locus is injectivity ([[def-self-transverse-immersion-and-double-point-locus]]), and an injective immersion from closed $M$ is an embedding by the proper injective immersion criterion ([[prop-a-proper-injective-immersion-is-a-smooth-embedding]]). Countable choice is inherited from the transversality items.

entry.title: Gauss frame map of an immersion into Euclidean space
entry.statement:
Let $f:M^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be a smooth immersion with $n\ge m$. Canonically trivializing the target tangent bundle makes its differential a smooth section
$$x\longmapsto df_x\quad\text{of}\quad\mathcal M=\operatorname{Mono}(TM,\varepsilon^n)\longrightarrow M,$$
whose fibre consists of injective linear maps $T_xM\to\mathbb R^n$, with the subspace smooth structure in the space of linear maps. This is the **unnormalized Gauss data** of $f$.

For a smooth local tangent frame $(s_1,\ldots,s_m)$, the **local Gauss frame map** is the full-rank matrix
$$g_U(x)=(df_xs_1(x)\mid\cdots\mid df_xs_m(x)).$$
A change of frame by $A(x)\in\mathrm{GL}_m(\mathbb R)$ changes this matrix to $g_U(x)A(x)$. These frame changes define the monomorphism bundle, and the smoothness of $df$ gives a smooth section in every such trivialization.

If a smooth tangent metric is supplied, write $E=V(TM,\varepsilon^n)$ for the separate bundle of **isometric** linear injections into the Euclidean target. Its fibre in an orthonormal tangent frame is the Stiefel manifold $V_m(\mathbb R^n)$. The **normalized Gauss section** is the fibrewise polar part
$$Q_f=df\,(df^*df)^{-1/2}\in\Gamma(E).$$
Positivity of $df^*df$, smoothness of its positive square root, and independence of orthonormal tangent frames are proved in [[prop-euclidean-formal-immersions-are-sections-of-a-stiefel-bundle]]. For an orthogonal change $U$ of tangent frame the normalized matrix changes to $Q_fU$. Ordinary Gram–Schmidt in an arbitrary frame does not supply this equivariant formula; polar normalization is the convention here.

A global tangent frame identifies $\mathcal M$ with the product bundle with fibre $\operatorname{Mono}(\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^n)$. Orthonormalizing that frame in the supplied metric identifies $E$ with the product bundle with fibre $V_m(\mathbb R^n)$, so the normalized section becomes a global map into that Stiefel manifold. Without a global frame it remains a section of $E$. Polar decomposition retains a positive-definite factor in the monomorphism fibre, and the cited proposition proves the resulting deformation retraction onto the Stiefel fibre. For $m=0$ both fibres are points; for $n=m$ they are respectively $\mathrm{GL}_m(\mathbb R)$ and $O(m)$.

No tangent metric is part of the unnormalized datum; normalization uses the supplied metric. No orientation, properness or normal framing is required. The normal bundle is the quotient $\varepsilon^n/df(TM)$ and is not part of these Gauss data. The model assertions in this definition are justified by the cited proposition, whose proof uses the raw full-rank matrix and frame-change definitions without assuming those assertions.
entry.strategy: Definition of the full monomorphism bundle and its separately metric-dependent normalized Stiefel model, with all normalization and section-space assertions justified by the existing direct consumer proposition.

entry.title: Euclidean formal immersions are sections of a Stiefel bundle
entry.statement:
Let $M^m$ be a smooth manifold, let $n\ge m$, and fix a smooth Riemannian metric on $TM$; such a metric exists under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, while the conclusions below require no additional choice once it is supplied. Give $\varepsilon^n=M\times\mathbb R^n$ its Euclidean metric. Distinguish the monomorphism bundle $\mathcal M=\operatorname{Mono}(TM,\varepsilon^n)$ from its orthonormal Stiefel subbundle $E=V(TM,\varepsilon^n)$, whose fibre is $V_m(\mathbb R^n)$, associated to the orthonormal frame bundle of $TM$. All section spaces carry the weak compact-open $C^\infty$ topology. Then:

1. Smooth bundle monomorphisms $B:TM\to\varepsilon^n$ over the identity correspond homeomorphically to $\Gamma(\mathcal M)$. Fibrewise polar normalization $B\mapsto B(B^*B)^{-1/2}$ gives an $O(m)$-equivariant strong deformation retraction $\Gamma(\mathcal M)\to\Gamma(E)$. In an orthonormal frame, the polar map is a diffeomorphism $\operatorname{Mono}(\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^n)\cong V_m(\mathbb R^n)\times\operatorname{Sym}^+_m$, where the second factor consists of positive-definite self-adjoint $m\times m$ matrices; thus the monomorphism fibre and the Stiefel fibre have the same homotopy type, rather than being identified homeomorphically.
2. The canonical target tangent trivialization gives the actual homeomorphism $\operatorname{FImm}(M,\mathbb R^n)\cong C^\infty(M,\mathbb R^n)\times\Gamma(\mathcal M)$. Contracting the first factor and polar-normalizing the second give a homotopy equivalence $\operatorname{FImm}(M,\mathbb R^n)\simeq\Gamma(E)$. In particular the two spaces have the same path components and homotopy invariants. Under the actual homeomorphism, the derivative map is $f\mapsto(f,df)$; in the normalized model it sends $df$ to its polar normalization.
3. For the standard metric on $S^m$, the bundle $E=V(TS^m,\varepsilon^n)$ is the pullback along $x\mapsto T_xS^m\in\mathrm{Gr}_m(\mathbb R^{m+1})$ of the bundle of isometric injections from the tautological $m$-plane to $\mathbb R^n$. Whenever $TM$ is trivial, $E$ is trivial; in particular $V(TS^1,\varepsilon^2)\cong S^1\times S^1$.

No orientation of $M$ or global tangent frame is needed. The normalization uses the supplied metric; metric existence for general $M$ is the only stated countable-choice use.
entry.strategy: The bundle of fibrewise injections of $TM$ into a trivial bundle is locally trivial: over a chart domain, a local frame of $TM$ and the standard frame of $\varepsilon^n$ present a bundle monomorphism as a smooth family of rank-$m$ $n\times m$ matrices, so the fibre is $\operatorname{Mono}(\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^n)\cong V_m(\mathbb R^n)$ and changes of frame act by right multiplication through $O(m)$. A smooth bundle map with injective fibres is the same thing as a smooth section of this bundle; both sides carry the compact-open $C^\infty$ topology on the corresponding mapping spaces, and in local matrices the two topologies have the same basic neighbourhoods. Clause 2 is clause 1 applied to the pair $(f,df)$ and the canonical trivialisation $T\mathbb R^n\cong\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$; injectivity of $df_x$ is exactly the immersion condition. Clause 3 is the defining universal property of the classifying map of $TS^m$: the frame bundle of $TS^m$ is the pullback of the universal principal $O(m)$-bundle, and passing to the associated Stiefel bundle gives the claim; a global frame trivialises the frame bundle and hence every associated bundle. This is the section-space description of [[def-space-of-immersions-and-space-of-formal-immersions]] in the Euclidean case, as used in the proof route of the design.

entry.title: The basepoint evaluation on the Stiefel section space is a fibration
entry.statement:
Let $1\le m\le n$, let $E=V(TS^m,\varepsilon^n)\to S^m$ be the orthonormal Stiefel model
of the section-space proposition with fibre $F=V_m(\mathbb R^n)$, let
$x_0\in S^m$, and let $\Gamma$ be the space of smooth sections of $E$ with the
weak compact-open $C^\infty$ topology and $\Gamma_*$ the subspace of sections that take a fixed
chosen value $s_0(x_0)\in E_{x_0}$. Then:

1. The evaluation map $\operatorname{ev}:\Gamma\to E_{x_0}$,
   $s\mapsto s(x_0)$, is a Hurewicz fibration with fibre $\Gamma_*$.
2. If $\Gamma_*\ne\varnothing$, a trivialisation of the pullback of $E$
   to the closed characteristic disk and a reference section identify
   $\Gamma_*$, up to homotopy, with the space of continuous based maps
   $(S^m,x_0)\to(V_m(\mathbb R^n),e_0)$; hence
   $\pi_0(\Gamma_*)\cong\pi_m(V_m(\mathbb R^n))$ whenever $\Gamma_*\ne\varnothing$;
   if $\Gamma\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge m+1$ then $\Gamma_*\ne\varnothing$ as
   well, because the fibre $F$ is path connected and evaluation is surjective
   on path components. Via this bijection the class of a section in
   $\pi_0(\Gamma_*)$ is its **difference class**: if two sections agree at
   $x_0$, the resulting transported disk models give based maps $S^m\to F$, and two
   sections are homotopic through sections fixed at $x_0$ exactly when these
   based maps are based-homotopic.
3. When $\Gamma_*\ne\varnothing$, base the fibration at a chosen section
   in $\Gamma_*$. Its long exact sequence yields an exact sequence of
   pointed sets
   $$\pi_1(V_m(\mathbb R^n))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\Gamma_*)\longrightarrow\pi_0(\Gamma)\longrightarrow\pi_0(V_m(\mathbb R^n));$$
   in particular, if $V_m(\mathbb R^n)$ is simply connected and
   $\Gamma\ne\varnothing$ then the difference class induces a non-canonical
   bijection $\pi_0(\Gamma)\cong\pi_m(V_m(\mathbb R^n))$, and if
   $\pi_m(V_m(\mathbb R^n))=0$, $n\ge m+1$ and $\Gamma\ne\varnothing$ then
   $\Gamma$ is path connected. The last conclusion requires a path-connected
   fibre; it is not asserted for $n=m$.
entry.strategy: For an empty section space, prove evaluation HLP vacuously; for a nonempty one, use O(n) local frame transport and a finite compact fibre cover. Compare fixed-value smooth and continuous sections by the explicit pinned smoothing operators, trivialize the pulled-back characteristic-disk bundle by the matrix ODE, and transport its generally nonconstant boundary map to a constant using a reference section and relative HLP. Obtain the based-map homotopy equivalence and difference classes only for a nonempty fixed-value fibre; apply the based exact sequence there, and retain the stated n>=m+1 and nonempty Gamma requirements for the final connectedness conclusion.

entry.title: Stiefel manifolds are connected, and simply connected in positive codimension
entry.statement: For $1\le m\le n$: (a) $V_m(\mathbb R^n)$ is path connected when $n\ge m+1$; (b) $\pi_1(V_m(\mathbb R^n))=0$ when $n\ge m+2$. In particular $V_m(\mathbb R^n)$ is simply connected for $n\ge m+2$, and $V_m(\mathbb R^{m+1})\cong SO(m+1)$ is connected, with $V_1(\mathbb R^k)=S^{k-1}$. No orientation of the frames is involved: $V_m(\mathbb R^n)$ is the space of ordered orthonormal $m$-frames.
entry.strategy: Proof by induction on $m$. The forgetful map $V_m(\mathbb R^n)\to V_1(\mathbb R^n)=S^{n-1}$, $(e_1,\dots,e_m)\mapsto e_1$, is the fibre bundle $SO(n)/SO(n-m)\to SO(n)/SO(n-1)=S^{n-1}$ with fibre $SO(n-1)/SO(n-m)\cong V_{m-1}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$; local triviality is the homogeneous-space fibration, which is numerable because $S^{n-1}$ is a CW complex, hence a Hurewicz fibration. For (a), the long exact sequence gives $\pi_0(V_{m-1}(\mathbb R^{n-1}))\to\pi_0(V_m(\mathbb R^n))\to\pi_0(S^{n-1})$; the outer terms vanish for $n\ge m+1\ge2$ by induction and by connectedness of spheres, so $\pi_0(V_m(\mathbb R^n))=0$; the base case $m=1$ is $S^{n-1}$ with $n\ge2$. For (b), the sequence gives $\pi_1(V_{m-1}(\mathbb R^{n-1}))\to\pi_1(V_m(\mathbb R^n))\to\pi_1(S^{n-1})$; for $n\ge m+2$ the induction hypothesis applies to $V_{m-1}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ because $n-1\ge (m-1)+2$, and $\pi_1(S^{n-1})=0$ for $n\ge3$ by the lower-dimensional nullhomotopy theorem; hence $\pi_1(V_m(\mathbb R^n))=0$. The base case $m=1$ is $S^{n-1}$ with $n\ge3$. The identification $V_m(\mathbb R^{m+1})\cong O(m+1)/O(1)\cong SO(m+1)$ is the quotient description in the definition of the Stiefel spaces. Countable choice is inherited from the numerable-bundle fibration theorem.

entry.title: The second homotopy group of SO(3) vanishes
entry.statement: $\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3),I)=0$. More precisely, for the two-sheeted covering homomorphism $\rho:S^3\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$, $\rho(q)(v)=qvq^{-1}$, from the unit quaternions onto the rotations of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$, the induced homomorphism $\rho_*:\pi_2(S^3,1)\to\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3),I)$ is a bijection and $\pi_2(S^3,1)=0$. Consequently also $\pi_2(O(3))=0$ and $\pi_2(V_2(\mathbb R^3))=0$, because $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v,u\times v)$ is a homeomorphism $V_2(\mathbb R^3)\to O(3)$ and $O(3)$ is the disjoint union of the two cosets of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, each homeomorphic to $\mathrm{SO}(3)$.
entry.strategy: Clause 2 of the quoted covering lemma states that for every covering projection $p:E\to B$ the induced map $p_*:\pi_n(E,e_0)\to\pi_n(B,p(e_0))$ is an isomorphism for every $n\ge2$; the quaternion double cover is constructed in the quoted example and its kernel and two-sheetedness are proved there. Hence $\rho_*:\pi_2(S^3,1)\to\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3),I)$ is an isomorphism. Every based map $S^2\to S^3$ is nullhomotopic by the lower-dimensional nullhomotopy theorem, so $\pi_2(S^3,1)=0$ and therefore $\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3),I)=0$. For the second sentence: $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v,u\times v)$ is a bijection from ordered orthonormal pairs to $O(3)$ (the third column is determined and the cross product identities give orthogonality and determinant $\pm1$), with inverse given by the first two columns, hence a homeomorphism; $O(3)$ is the disjoint union of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and the coset of a reflection, and left translation identifies each coset with $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, so the inclusion induces isomorphisms on all homotopy groups. The argument makes only finitely many choices and uses no choice principle beyond the published suppliers.

entry.title: Rotation number of an immersed oriented circle in the plane
entry.statement:
Let $S^1$ be oriented and parametrised as $\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with the
positive orientation, let $\partial_\theta$ be the corresponding positively
oriented unit tangent vector field of $S^1$, and let $f:S^1\to\mathbb R^2$ be a
smooth immersion, that is, a regular closed curve
([[def-immersion-submersion-and-constant-rank-map]],
[[def-smooth-manifold]]). Writing $T\mathbb R^2\cong\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2$
for the canonical identification, the differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]], [[def-tangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]])
gives for each $\theta$ the velocity vector $df_\theta(\partial_\theta)$, which
is nonzero because $f$ is an immersion.

The **normalised velocity**, or unit tangent, of $f$ is the map
$$\tau_f:S^1\longrightarrow S^1,\qquad \tau_f(\theta)=\frac{df_\theta(\partial_\theta)}{\lvert df_\theta(\partial_\theta)\rvert},$$
which is continuous because the velocity never vanishes and every nonzero
vector is a positive multiple of a unique unit vector.

The **rotation number** (also **rotation index**) of $f$ is
$$\operatorname{rot}(f):=\deg(\tau_f)\in\mathbb Z,$$
the degree of the unit tangent map. Concretely, after choosing the base point
$\theta_0=[0]$, identifying the unit circle with $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ by the
standard parametrisation and rotating the *target* circle by a constant so that
$\tau_f(\theta_0)$ corresponds to $[0]$, the class of $\tau_f$ is a based loop
in the sense of [[def-degree-of-a-circle-loop]], and its degree is the integer
$\operatorname{rot}(f)$; the constant rotation of the target plane changes
neither the winding number nor the degree, and the degree descends to based
loop classes ([[cor-degree-descends-to-circle-loop-classes]]), so the value is
independent of the choice of $\theta_0$ and of the lift used to compute it
([[thm-circle-loops-are-path-homotopic-iff-they-have-equal-degree]]).

Equivalent formulations, all taking the same value:

- The velocity curve $t\mapsto f'(t)$ is a closed $C^1$, hence rectifiable,
  loop in $\mathbb C^\times=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, and
  $\operatorname{rot}(f)$ is its **winding number about the origin**: the
  normalised velocity $t\mapsto f'(t)/\lvert f'(t)\rvert$ is exactly
  $\tau_f$, and after the constant rotation
  $\gamma\mapsto\gamma/\gamma(t_0)$ of the target plane, which changes neither
  the winding number about $0$ nor the degree of the normalised loop,
  [[thm-winding-number-equals-circle-degree]] identifies $n(\gamma,0)$ with the
  degree of the normalised loop, while
  [[cor-winding-number-classifies-loops-in-the-punctured-plane]] identifies that
  winding number with the class in $\pi_1(\mathbb C^\times,1)\cong\mathbb Z$.
- $\operatorname{rot}(f)$ equals $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ times the **total signed
  turning angle** of the tangent, i.e. the rotation index of the regular closed
  plane curve $f$ in the sense of
  [[def-rotation-index-of-a-regular-closed-plane-curve]], where the tangent
  angle is lifted continuously and the corner jumps are zero for a smooth
  curve.

The normalisation is fixed by the round unit circle: the immersion
$\theta\mapsto(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ traversed once in the positive direction
has unit tangent $(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$ winding once positively, hence rotation number $+1$, and its reverse has
rotation number $-1$. Reversing the orientation of the domain negates the
rotation number, while a regular (orientation-preserving) reparametrisation
leaves it unchanged; for the tangent-angle model these two facts are part of
the well-definedness statement of
[[def-rotation-index-of-a-regular-closed-plane-curve]].

No convexity, simplicity, self-intersection restriction or properness is
imposed; $\operatorname{rot}$ is an invariant of the oriented immersed circle,
not of its image.
entry.strategy: Definition. The rotation number is the degree of the unit tangent map; the identification with the winding number of the velocity is positive pointwise normalisation, and the identification with the total signed turning angle is the standard unwinding of the argument. Well-definedness (independence of the regular parametrisation and the sign under orientation reversal) is proved in the stated degree items, not here; nothing else is claimed.

references.title: Hassler Whitney, On regular closed curves in the plane, Compositio Mathematica 4 (1937), pp. 276–284, §1 (rotation number and invariance), §2 (Theorem 1, deformation theorem) and §3 (Lemma 2, Theorem 2)
John Francis, The h-Principle, Lecture 10: Classifying immersions of spheres, after Smale (notes by A. Beaudry), PDF pp. 1–2

entry.title: Formal immersions of the circle in the plane are classified by the winding number
entry.statement:
Let $E=V(TS^1,\varepsilon^2)\to S^1$ be the Stiefel bundle of the
section-space proposition for $M=S^1$ and $n=2$, with fibre
$V_1(\mathbb R^2)=S^1$. Then $E\cong S^1\times S^1$ is trivial, its section
space $\Gamma$ is homeomorphic to $C^\infty(S^1,S^1)$ with the weak smooth topology, and
$\pi_0(\Gamma)\cong\mathbb Z$ by degree. The resulting **winding invariant**
$w(f,F)\in\mathbb Z$ of a formal immersion $(f,F)$ is the degree of the section
expressed in a fixed trivialisation; for the derivative $(f,df)$ of an
immersion it equals the rotation number $\operatorname{rot}(f)$ of the
preceding definition. Two formal immersions of $S^1$ into $\mathbb R^2$ lie in
the same path component of $\operatorname{FImm}(S^1,\mathbb R^2)$ if and only
if their winding invariants are equal.
entry.strategy: The tangent bundle of the circle is trivial, so a global frame trivialises the frame bundle and, by the proposition, the associated bundle of injections: $E\cong S^1\times S^1$, and sections of a product bundle over $S^1$ are exactly maps $S^1\to S^1$. Their homotopy classes are the degree, by the circle degree classification. In this trivialisation the second component of $(f,df)$ is the velocity $df(\partial_\theta)$ up to the identification of $TS^1$ with $S^1\times\mathbb R$; dividing by the smooth positive function $\lvert df(\partial_\theta)\rvert$ is a homotopy of nowhere-zero sections, so the class of the section is the class of the unit tangent map, which is the rotation number.

entry.title: Regular homotopy preserves the formal Gauss class
entry.statement: Let $M^m,N^n$ be smooth manifolds with $m\le n$ (no compactness of $M$ is needed for this invariance) and let $H:M\times[0,1]\to N$ be a regular homotopy, that is, a smooth map whose restriction $H_t$ to every slice is an immersion. Then $t\mapsto(H_t,dH_t)$ is a continuous path in $\operatorname{FImm}(M,N)$ for the weak compact-open $C^\infty$ topology, and consequently every homotopy invariant of formal data is constant along a regular homotopy: the path component of $(H_t,dH_t)$ in $\operatorname{FImm}(M,N)$ does not depend on $t$. For $M=S^m,N=\mathbb R^n$ this invariant is the Gauss frame class of the preceding items (the difference class in $\pi_m(V_m(\mathbb R^n))$ when $n\ge m+2$); for $M=S^1,N=\mathbb R^2$ it is the winding number, i.e. the rotation number. In particular two regularly homotopic immersions have homotopic formal data, which is the necessity half of every classification on this page.
entry.strategy: Prove weak continuity of the smooth homotopy adjoint directly on finitely many compact chart pieces. Around each reference time t0, first choose a compact relative time neighbourhood J keeping all image pieces in their prescribed target charts, then apply uniform continuity to finitely many coordinate derivatives on K_i times J. Compose with the continuous derivative map and use constancy of a path component; the compact-source converse remains the separate smoothing interface.

entry.title: Whitney–Graustein classification of plane circle immersions
entry.statement: Let $f,g:S^1\to\mathbb R^2$ be oriented immersions of the circle (regular closed curves). Then $f$ and $g$ are regularly homotopic through immersions if and only if their rotation numbers agree, $\operatorname{rot}(f)=\operatorname{rot}(g)$. Equivalently, the rotation number induces a bijection $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}(S^1,\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb Z$; every integer is realised by the $k$-fold positively or negatively oriented round circle, and the invariant detects the orientation: the reverse of a curve with rotation number $k$ has rotation number $-k$, so a circle cannot be turned inside out in the plane through immersions.
entry.strategy: Necessity: a regular homotopy gives a continuous path of formal data (the invariance lemma), and the winding invariant of the circle lemma is constant along such a path and equals the rotation number; hence regularly homotopic immersions have equal rotation numbers. Sufficiency: if the rotation numbers agree, the formal data of $f$ and $g$ have the same winding invariant and are therefore homotopic through formal immersions; the Smale\u2013Hirsch theorem gives a weak homotopy equivalence $\operatorname{Imm}(S^1,\mathbb R^2)\to\operatorname{FImm}(S^1,\mathbb R^2)$ (positive codimension $1<2$, closed compact source), hence a bijection on path components, so $f$ and $g$ are regularly homotopic. The classical deformation proof of [[whit37]] deforms the velocity through nonvanishing fields with prescribed total turning and then corrects the average; the two routes prove the same statement. The realisation of all integers and the sign under orientation reversal are the explicit $k$-fold circle computations. Countable choice is inherited from the Smale\u2013Hirsch supplier.

entry.title: Smale classification of sphere immersions in Euclidean space
entry.statement:
Let $1\le m\le n$, let $F=V_m(\mathbb R^n)\cong O(n)/O(n-m)$ be the Stiefel
manifold of orthonormal $m$-frames, and let
$E=V(TS^m,\varepsilon^n)\to S^m$ be the Stiefel bundle of the section-space
proposition. Its sections are the fibrewise-injection part of the formal
non-holonomic data, and the projection
$\operatorname{FImm}(S^m,\mathbb R^n)\to\Gamma(E)$ forgetting the underlying
map and polar-normalizing the fibrewise injection is a homotopy equivalence, so path components of $\Gamma(E)$ and of
$\operatorname{FImm}(S^m,\mathbb R^n)$ agree.

1. If $n\ge m+2$, then $F$ is simply connected, $E$ admits sections (because
   $TS^m\oplus\varepsilon^{n-m}\cong\varepsilon^n$), and the difference class of
   the evaluation lemma induces a non-canonical bijection
   $\pi_0\Gamma(E)\cong\pi_m(V_m(\mathbb R^n))=\pi_m(O(n)/O(n-m))$. Since the
   Smale–Hirsch derivative map is a weak homotopy equivalence, the same set
   classifies regular homotopy classes of immersions: there is a non-canonical
   bijection between regular homotopy classes of immersions
   $S^m\to\mathbb R^n$ and $\pi_m(O(n)/O(n-m))$, realised by the clutching
   difference class of the tangent framings.
2. If $n=m+1$, then $V_m(\mathbb R^{m+1})\cong\mathrm{SO}(m+1)$ and the
   difference class gives a non-canonical bijection
   $\pi_m(\mathrm{SO}(m+1))\to\pi_0\Gamma(E)\cong\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}(S^m,\mathbb R^{m+1})$;
   in particular, if $\pi_m(\mathrm{SO}(m+1))=0$ then all immersions
   $S^m\to\mathbb R^{m+1}$ are regularly homotopic.
3. The instances used on this page: $m=1$, $n=2$, where
   $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}(S^1,\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb Z$ with the rotation
   number as invariant; and $m=2$, $n=3$, where
   $\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3))=0$ and hence all immersions $S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ are
   regularly homotopic.
entry.strategy: Clause 1: the fibre is simply connected by the Stiefel connectivity lemma; the difference-class bijection is the evaluation lemma; sections exist because the tangent bundle of the sphere is stably trivial, $TS^m\oplus\varepsilon^1\cong\varepsilon^{m+1}$, which is the tangent-normal identity applied to the standard embedding together with the triviality of the normal line, and adding $n-m-1$ trivial summands gives a bundle monomorphism $TS^m\to\varepsilon^n$; the immersion statement is the induced bijection on path components of the Smale\u2013Hirsch weak homotopy equivalence. Clause 2: $V_m(\mathbb R^{m+1})=O(m+1)/O(1)\cong SO(m+1)$ and the exact sequence of the evaluation lemma exhibits $\pi_0\Gamma(E)$ as a quotient of $\pi_0(\Gamma_*)\cong\pi_m(SO(m+1))$ because $\pi_0(F)=0$; the specialisation $m=2$ uses the vanishing of $\pi_2(SO(3))$. The circle instance is the separate circle computation. These are the statements of Smale's classification of sphere immersions (Francis Lecture 10, Theorem 0.2 and Corollary 0.3; Cohen Theorem 5), with the clutching/tangent condition printed explicitly. Countable choice is inherited from Smale\u2013Hirsch.

entry.title: Standard and reflected two-sphere immersions have homotopic formal data in $\mathbb R^3$
entry.statement:
Let $\iota:S^2\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^3$ be the standard inclusion of the unit
sphere and let $a:S^2\to S^2$, $a(x)=-x$, be the antipodal map; equivalently
replace $\iota$ by $r\circ\iota$ for a reflection $r$ of $\mathbb R^3$, which
differs from $\iota\circ a$ by an orientation-preserving rotation of the
target. Then the formal immersions $(\iota,d\iota)$ and
$(\iota\circ a,d(\iota\circ a))$ lie in the same path component of
$\operatorname{FImm}(S^2,\mathbb R^3)$. More precisely, after trivialising the
Stiefel bundle $V(TS^2,\varepsilon^3)$ over the two hemispheres, the difference
of the two Gauss frame sections over the equator glues to a continuous map
$F:S^2\to V_2(\mathbb R^3)\cong\mathrm{SO}(3)$ whose homotopy class in
$\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3))$ measures the obstruction to homotoping the formal data;
since $\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3))=0$ and $O(3)$ is the disjoint union of two copies
of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, also $\pi_2(O(3))=0$, $F$ is nullhomotopic, and the two
formal data are homotopic. This vanishing is the algebraic content of the
eversion.
entry.strategy: The bundle $E=V(TS^2,\varepsilon^3)$ admits the section $d\iota$, so $\Gamma(E)\ne\varnothing$; its fibre $V_2(\mathbb R^3)\cong O(3)$ is connected and has $\pi_2=0$, so by the evaluation lemma $\pi_0\Gamma(E)$ is a quotient of $\pi_2(V_2(\mathbb R^3))=0$, that is, $\Gamma(E)$ is path connected; hence all formal immersions of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$, in particular those of $\iota$ and of its reflection, are homotopic. The explicit description of the difference as the gluing of the two hemispherical framings along the equator is the clutching construction in the sources; when the bundle is trivialised over each hemisphere the obstruction is the class of a map $S^2\to V_2(\mathbb R^3)$, and the class vanishes because the group is null in degree two. Countable choice is inherited from the evaluation-fibration supplier.

entry.title: Sphere eversion
entry.statement: The standard embedding $\iota:S^2\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^3$ is regularly homotopic, through immersions $S^2\to\mathbb R^3$, to its inside-out reflection $\iota\circ a$ (equivalently to $r\circ\iota$ for a reflection $r$ of $\mathbb R^3$). More precisely, every two immersions $S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ are regularly homotopic: the space $\operatorname{Imm}(S^2,\mathbb R^3)$ is path connected, and a regular homotopy from $\iota$ to $\iota\circ a$ cannot be chosen through embeddings.
entry.strategy: The formal data of the two immersions are homotopic by the preceding lemma. The Smale\u2013Hirsch derivative map $\operatorname{Imm}(S^2,\mathbb R^3)\to\operatorname{FImm}(S^2,\mathbb R^3)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence ($2<3$, compact closed source, positive codimension), hence induces a bijection on $\pi_0$; a weak homotopy equivalence also induces a bijection between the sets of path components, so the two immersions lie in one path component of the immersion space, i.e. are regularly homotopic. Alternatively the classification theorem clause 2 with $\pi_2(SO(3))=0$ gives the path connectivity of the whole immersion space directly. The last sentence is the separate remark on isotopies through embeddings. Countable choice is inherited from Smale\u2013Hirsch.

entry.title: Sphere eversion cannot be an isotopy through embeddings
entry.statement: No homotopy from $\iota$ to $\iota\circ a$ (or to $r\circ\iota$) through embeddings of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ exists, so every eversion contains slices that are not injective; self-intersections are unavoidable. The invariant is the coorientation: an embedding of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ bounds a ball, and along a continuous family of embeddings the bounded complementary component varies continuously (Jordan\u2013Brouwer separation), so the normal direction pointing into the bounded side and the orientation of the parametrisation relative to it are locally constant; $\iota$ has the positively oriented parametrisation with respect to the outward normal while $\iota\circ a$ and $r\circ\iota$ have the opposite sign, so $\iota$ and $\iota\circ a$ lie in different path components of $\operatorname{Emb}(S^2,\mathbb R^3)$. Equivalently, an ambient isotopy of $\mathbb R^3$ preserves the side of the image, whereas eversion reverses the inside/outside labelling. Regular homotopy is strictly coarser than isotopy here: the two maps are in one path component of $\operatorname{Imm}(S^2,\mathbb R^3)$ by the eversion theorem and in different path components of $\operatorname{Emb}(S^2,\mathbb R^3)$.
entry.strategy: Remark. The first sentence is proved by the coorientation sign described in the statement; a homotopy through embeddings would be a path of embeddings, along which the bounded complementary component and the orientation sign of the parametrisation with respect to the outward normal are continuous, hence constant, while the sign changes from $+1$ for the standard inclusion to $-1$ for its antipodal or reflected version. The separation fact used is the Jordan\u2013Brouwer theorem for a smoothly embedded two-sphere; no proof of the eversion is repeated here. P: not-applicable (recorded remark).

entry.title: Regular homotopy allows self-intersections but never a rank drop
entry.statement: A regular homotopy $H:M\times[0,1]\to N$ of immersions requires every slice $H_t$ to be immersive: the rank of $dH_t$ is $\dim M$ at every point of every slice, and no slice may contain a point of rank drop, a cusp of the parametrised family or a point whose derivative degenerates. Self-intersections, by contrast, are permitted: an immersion may identify two distinct points $x\ne y$ with $H_t(x)=H_t(y)$ provided the images of $T_xM$ and $T_yM$ are distinct linear subspaces; immersions are only required to be locally injective. During an eversion of $S^2$ in $\mathbb R^3$ the slices must acquire self-intersections and cannot be embeddings (the preceding remark), while no slice may have a rank drop, so the two phenomena are logically independent. The immersion condition is open in the strong topology on a compact source, so a rank drop can only occur by leaving that open set.
entry.strategy: Remark. It fixes the exact meaning of the family condition: the fibrewise injectivity of $dH_t$ is a pointwise condition on each slice, whereas injectivity of $H_t$ is not a local differential condition and is never required. The openness statement is the published open-immersion-loci item. P: not-applicable (recorded remark).

entry.title: Sphere immersion groups are AT computations, not DT constructions
entry.statement: The homotopy-theoretic inputs used on this page \u2014 $\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3))=0$ and $\pi_1(\mathrm{SO}(2))\cong\mathbb Z$ through the quaternion double cover and the covering isomorphism on $\pi_n$ for $n\ge2$, the Stiefel connectivities $\pi_0(V_m(\mathbb R^n))=0$ for $n\ge m+1$ and $\pi_1(V_m(\mathbb R^n))=0$ for $n\ge m+2$, and the higher homotopy exact sequences of the fibrations $V_m(\mathbb R^n)\to S^{n-1}$ and $O(n-m)\to O(n)$ \u2014 are algebraic-topology computations owned by [[higher-homotopy-groups-and-cofiber-sequences]], [[fibrations-fiber-bundles-and-homotopy-exact-sequences]], [[covering-spaces-and-lifting]] and [[hurewicz-whitehead-freudenthal-and-cw-approximation]]. This page consumes them and contributes only the differential-topological reduction: the Smale\u2013Hirsch weak homotopy equivalence (from the predecessor page), the identification of formal data with Stiefel sections, and the clutching difference class that turns the classification into these groups. No new homotopy-theoretic machinery is minted here, and conversely the groups $\pi_m(V_m(\mathbb R^n))$ remain AT-owned inputs; each use is recorded in the dependencies of the items above.
entry.strategy: Remark. It records the ownership seam of the design's warning: DT consumes the Stiefel homotopy groups and does not construct them, and the very definition of the groups, the long exact sequences and the covering isomorphisms live on the named AT pages. P: not-applicable (recorded remark).

entry.title: Plane circle immersions of rotation number $k$
entry.statement: For every integer $k\ne0$ the map $\gamma_k:S^1\to\mathbb R^2$, $\gamma_k(\theta)=(\cos k\theta,\sin k\theta)$, with $S^1=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ positively oriented, is an immersion: $\gamma_k'(\theta)=k(-\sin k\theta,\cos k\theta)$ never vanishes. Its unit tangent map is $\theta\mapsto(-\sin k\theta,\cos k\theta)$, the $k$-th power of the standard unit-speed circle map, of degree $k$; hence $\operatorname{rot}(\gamma_k)=k$. For $k<0$ this is the $|k|$-fold circle traversed in the negative direction, so the construction realises every nonzero integer. The remaining value $k=0$ is realised by the Gerono lemniscate $\delta(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin2\theta)$, whose velocity $(-\sin\theta,2\cos2\theta)$ is nonvanishing: the positive $x$-axis of the velocity plane is met exactly twice, at $\theta=5\pi/4$ and $\theta=7\pi/4$, with opposite signed crossing directions, so the winding is $0$ and $\operatorname{rot}(\delta)=0$. By the Whitney\u2013Graustein theorem, $\gamma_k$ and $\gamma_l$ are regularly homotopic if and only if $k=l$, and the family $\{\gamma_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}\cup\{\delta\}$ contains exactly one regular homotopy class for each rotation number.
entry.strategy: Direct computation: the derivative of $\gamma_k$ is displayed and nonvanishing, and the unit tangent map is the $k$-fold power of the identity loop, whose degree is $k$ by the power-map degree computation; for the lemniscate the velocity is nonvanishing and its winding is computed by counting signed crossings of a ray, giving zero. The classification statement is the Whitney\u2013Graustein theorem. Countable choice is inherited through the classification theorem.

entry.title: The figure eight and the round circle are not regularly homotopic as oriented immersions
entry.statement:
**False claim:** any two oriented immersed circles in the plane are regularly
homotopic; in particular the Gerono lemniscate and the round circle, despite
both being simple closed pictures of one loop, represent the same regular
homotopy class.

The claim fails because the regular homotopy invariant of oriented immersed
circles is the rotation number, which is not changed by bending, translating or
self-crossing moves but jumps between the two curves in question.
entry.strategy: The two rotation numbers are computed in the companion example: the lemniscate's velocity has winding zero and the circle's unit tangent map has degree one. They differ, so the classification theorem separates the two classes. The remark about the doubly traversed circle is the explicit family $\gamma_2$ from the same example. This is the design's intended use: self-intersection count is not the invariant.

entry.title: Formal frame homotopy behind sphere eversion
entry.statement: Let $\iota:S^2\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^3$ be the standard embedding and $\iota\circ a$ its antipodal version. Trivialise the Stiefel bundle $V(TS^2,\varepsilon^3)$ over the closed upper and lower hemispheres (contractible, hence chart domains with coordinate frames); the Gauss frame sections of $d\iota$ and of $d(\iota\circ a)$ then agree near the poles and differ over the equator by a loop of frames, and gluing the upper section to the lower section twisted by that loop yields a continuous map $F:S^2\to V_2(\mathbb R^3)\cong O(3)$. Since $S^2$ is simply connected, $F$ lifts along the two-sheeted covering $\rho:S^3\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$ to a map $\widetilde F:S^2\to S^3$; every based map $S^2\to S^3$ is nullhomotopic, and projecting a nullhomotopy gives a nullhomotopy of $F$. Hence the difference class $[F]\in\pi_2(O(3))=\pi_2(\mathrm{SO}(3))$ is zero and the two formal framings are homotopic. This finite check \u2014 a lift through the quaternion double cover plus $\pi_2(S^3)=0$ \u2014 is the algebraic input that the eversion theorem converts into a genuine regular homotopy of immersions.
entry.strategy: The hemisphere triviality, the gluing loop and the resulting map $F$ are the clutching description of the formal difference class of the preceding lemma; the covering lifting criterion applies because $S^2$ is simply connected and locally path connected, and the homotopy lifting property of a covering lifts nullhomotopies back; the nullhomotopy of $\widetilde F$ exists because $\pi_2(S^3)=0$. Projecting it along $\rho$ gives the nullhomotopy of $F$, so the difference class vanishes. Countable choice is inherited through the suppliers.

entry.title: A homotopy through maps with a rank drop is not a regular homotopy
entry.statement: Define $H:S^1\times[0,1]\to\mathbb R^2$ by $H_t(\theta)=((1-t)\cos\theta+t,(1-t)\sin\theta)$. For every $t<1$ the slice $H_t$ is an immersion, because its derivative $(-(1-t)\sin\theta,(1-t)\cos\theta)$ has norm $1-t$ and never vanishes, and $H_0$ is the standard unit circle. But $H_1$ is the constant map at $(1,0)$, with $dH_1=0$ at every point: the family has a rank drop at the final time. Hence $H$ is a smooth homotopy through maps from an immersion to a non-immersion that is immersive at every earlier time, and it is not a regular homotopy and cannot be used to conclude any regular-homotopy statement; in particular it does not show that the circle is regularly homotopic to a point. The example separates the two conditions used on this page: slicewise rank $\dim M$ for every time (regular homotopy) versus mere continuity of the family (arbitrary homotopy).
entry.strategy: Direct computation of the derivative of $H_t$ shows it vanishes identically exactly at $t=1$; for $t<1$ it has constant norm $1-t>0$, so each earlier slice is an immersion. A regular homotopy would require the final slice to be immersive, which it is not. This is the design's pinch-a-circle test for the rank-drop remark.

entry.title: A Boy surface immersion of real projective two-space
entry.statement: There is a smooth immersion $\beta:\mathbb{RP}^2\to\mathbb R^3$ whose image is Boy's surface. The Bryant\u2013Kusner parametrisation of it is given on the closed unit disk $\lvert w\rvert\le1$ by the real and imaginary parts of the rational expressions displayed in the sources, followed by inversion in the unit sphere; it satisfies $P(w)=P(-1/w^\star)$ in general and $P(w)=P(-w)$ on the boundary circle, so it descends to the quotient of the disk by the antipodal boundary identification, which is $\mathbb{RP}^2$, and it has injective differential, so $\beta$ is an immersion (Kusner verifies immersedness explicitly for the minimal surface, and inversion in the unit sphere is a local diffeomorphism away from the origin; the three planar ends close smoothly at the triple point under inversion). Every immersion $f:\mathbb{RP}^2\to\mathbb R^3$ has nontrivial normal line bundle: a global nonvanishing normal field $n$ together with the standard orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ would orient the tangent planes by declaring a basis $(v_1,v_2)$ of $T_x\mathbb{RP}^2$ positive exactly when $(v_1,v_2,n(x))$ is a positive basis of $T_{f(x)}\mathbb R^3$, contradicting nonorientability of $\mathbb{RP}^2$; equivalently $w_1(\nu_f)=w_1(T\mathbb{RP}^2)\ne0$ for the tautological generator. Boy's surface is therefore the exact analogue in codimension one of the phenomenon that a nonorientable hypersurface has no global normal side, and it has self-intersections because an injective immersion of a compact manifold would be an embedding and a closed nonorientable surface does not embed in $\mathbb R^3$.
entry.strategy: The parametrisation and the inversion construction are taken from the cited Kusner\u2013Karcher treatments; immersedness is the explicit verification for the odd-p minimal surfaces of Kusner (p=3) together with the standard fact that inversion is a local diffeomorphism off the origin and that a planar end closes smoothly to a triple point. The normal-bundle argument is the elementary coorientation computation in the statement; the last sentence uses that a proper injective immersion of a compact manifold is an embedding and that a closed nonorientable surface cannot embed in $\mathbb R^3$ as a hypersurface (the mod-two separation argument).

entry.title: Stable normal inverse of the tangent bundle
entry.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth $m$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). A **stable normal inverse of the tangent bundle** is a pair $(
u,\varphi)$ consisting of a smooth real vector bundle $
u	o M$ of finite rank $k$ ([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]]) and a smooth bundle isomorphism
$$\varphi:TM\oplus
u\longrightarrow\varepsilon^{m+k}$$
onto the trivial real bundle $\varepsilon^{m+k}=M	imes\mathbb R^{m+k}$ ([[def-tangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]], [[def-whitney-sum-of-vector-bundles]], [[def-vector-bundle-map-section-subbundle-and-isomorphism]]). A **rank-$k$ stable normal inverse** is one whose bundle has rank $k$; when the rank is not named, $k=\operatorname{rank}
u$. Two stable normal inverses $(
u_0,\varphi_0)$, $(
u_1,\varphi_1)$ are **stably equivalent** when $
u_0\oplus\varepsilon^{a}\cong
u_1\oplus\varepsilon^{b}$ for some $a,b\ge0$. Adding a trivial summand, $(
u,\varphi)\mapsto(
u\oplus\varepsilon^{1},\varphi\oplus\operatorname{id}_{\varepsilon^{1}})$, carries rank-$k$ inverses to rank-$(k+1)$ inverses and preserves stable equivalence.

This is the inverse-bundle form of the published stable normal bundle [[def-stable-normal-bundle-of-a-compact-smooth-manifold]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for compact $M$ and a smooth embedding $i:M\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$ with $N\ge m$, the normal bundle gives a rank-$(N-m)$ example with $TM\oplus
u_i\cong\varepsilon^N$ (the $N>m$ case is [[lem-an-embedding-into-r-n-gives-the-same-normal-bundle-identity]]; for $N=m$, $di$ is a fibrewise isomorphism and the normal quotient is the zero bundle). The dimension qualification is needed for an empty source, whose fibrewise immersion condition alone imposes no dimension inequality. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ every closed smooth $M$ has such an inverse by [[lem-an-embedding-into-r-n-gives-the-same-normal-bundle-identity]]. The converse statement that every stable normal inverse is stably isomorphic to the normal bundle of an embedding is the stable classification statement; it is neither asserted nor used on this page. No choice principle is part of the definition; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ enters only through the metric and tubular identifications of the cited embedding lemma.
entry.strategy:
Definition fixing the exact object the page computes with. It separates the inverse bundle $
u$ together with its isomorphism $\varphi:TM\oplus
u	o\varepsilon^{m+k}$ from the stable equivalence class, so that the rank of $
u$ (the codimension in an immersion problem) is part of the data while the characteristic classes of $
u$ are proved below to be independent of the choice. The stabilization clause is the operation corresponding to adding trivial summands in the published stable normal bundle. Nothing is proved here; existence for closed $M$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the separately inventoried justification lemma [[lem-an-embedding-into-r-n-gives-the-same-normal-bundle-identity]], and the independence of the characteristic classes is [[lem-normal-stiefel-whitney-class-is-the-multiplicative-inverse-of-the-tangent-class]] and [[lem-normal-pontryagin-class-is-the-rational-inverse-of-the-tangent-pontryagin-class]].

entry.title: The pullback of a trivial smooth vector bundle is canonically trivial
entry.statement: Let $f:N\to M$ be a smooth map and let $\varepsilon^r_M=M\times\mathbb R^r$ be the trivial smooth real rank-$r$ bundle over $M$. Then the pullback $f^*\varepsilon^r_M$ is canonically isomorphic to the trivial bundle $\varepsilon^r_N=N\times\mathbb R^r$: the constant frame $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $\varepsilon^r_M$ pulls back to the nowhere-zero global frame $x\mapsto(x,e_j)$ of $f^*\varepsilon^r_M$, and the isomorphism is the one determined by that frame ([[def-local-frame-and-global-frame-of-a-vector-bundle]], [[cor-a-vector-bundle-is-trivial-if-and-only-if-it-has-a-global-frame]]). This product-bundle assertion is choice-free.
entry.strategy:
1.1 Define $\Phi:f^*\varepsilon^r_M\to N\times\mathbb R^r$ by $\Phi(q,(f(q),v))=(q,v)$, using the description [F1]. Then $\Phi$ is well defined, and its inverse is $(q,v)\mapsto(q,(f(q),v))$. On each fibre it is the linear isomorphism onto $\{q\}\times\mathbb R^r$ inverse to $v\mapsto(f(q),v)$, and $\Phi$ lies over $\operatorname{id}_N$. So $\Phi$ is a fibrewise-linear bijection over the base. [F1, F4]

2.1 $\Phi$ is smooth with smooth inverse. Indeed, in the global pullback chart of [F2] coming from the global chart $\Phi(p,v)=(p,v)$ of $\varepsilon^r_M$, the chart map is exactly $\Phi$, i.e. the identity identification of $N\times\mathbb R^r$; and the inverse $(q,v)\mapsto(q,(f(q),v))$ has components $q\mapsto q$, $q\mapsto f(q)$ and $v\mapsto v$, which are smooth by [F4] since $f$ is smooth. Hence $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism, and consequently a smooth bundle isomorphism over $N$. [F2, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Therefore $f^*\varepsilon^r_M\cong\varepsilon^r_N$ as smooth vector bundles over $N$, by the isomorphism $\Phi$, which was defined by an explicit formula using only $f$ and hence is canonical. Equivalently, the constant sections $s_j(p)=(p,e_j)$ of $\varepsilon^r_M$ pull back to the sections $f^*s_j(q)=(q,(f(q),e_j))$ of $f^*\varepsilon^r_M$, none of whose values is the zero vector; these pullbacks are smooth because in the global pullback chart of step 2.1 the section $f^*s_j$ reads as the constant map $q\mapsto e_j$, and they form a global frame of $f^*\varepsilon^r_M$ that $\Phi$ converts into the standard frame of $N\times\mathbb R^r$. No selection of local trivializations, complements or representatives has been made: the chart of [F2] used above is the single global chart of the product bundle, so the argument uses no choice principle. The case $r=0$ gives the zero bundle over $N$, and the empty or disconnected base is covered verbatim. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

entry.title: The pullback of the Euclidean tangent bundle is canonically trivial
entry.statement: Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f:N\to\mathbb R^r$ be a smooth map. Under the standard-coordinate identification $T\mathbb R^r\cong\varepsilon^r_{\mathbb R^r}$ given by the induced tangent chart of the identity chart ([[thm-the-tangent-bundle-has-a-canonical-smooth-2n-manifold-structure]], [[def-induced-tangent-bundle-chart]]), the pullback tangent bundle is canonically trivial: $$f^*T\mathbb R^r\cong f^*\varepsilon^r_{\mathbb R^r}\cong\varepsilon^r_N,$$ where the second isomorphism pulls back the constant frame by [[lem-pullback-of-a-trivial-smooth-vector-bundle-is-canonically-trivial]].
entry.strategy:
1.1 The identity $\operatorname{id}:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R^r$ is a smooth chart whose domain is all of $\mathbb R^r$, so by [F1] its induced tangent-bundle chart $\widetilde{\operatorname{id}}:T\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^r$, $v\mapsto(p,v^1,\dots,v^r)$, is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^r$; it is linear on every fibre. Hence it is a smooth bundle isomorphism $$T\mathbb R^r\longrightarrow\varepsilon^r_{\mathbb R^r}=\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^r,$$ the standard-coordinate identification. It is determined by the identity chart alone, so no choice is made in exhibiting it. [F1]

2.1 Pulling this identification back along $f$ gives a smooth bundle isomorphism $f^*T\mathbb R^r\cong f^*\varepsilon^r_{\mathbb R^r}$ over $N$, and [F2] gives a canonical isomorphism $f^*\varepsilon^r_{\mathbb R^r}\cong\varepsilon^r_N$ carrying the pulled-back constant frame to the standard frame. Composing, $$f^*T\mathbb R^r\cong f^*\varepsilon^r_{\mathbb R^r}\cong\varepsilon^r_N$$ canonically. The only choice principle used is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, inherited through [F1]; the pullback comparison of [F2] is choice-free, and the empty or disconnected case of $N$ is included since all maps displayed are evaluated fibrewise. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

entry.title: Positive intermediate cohomology of compactified Euclidean space vanishes
entry.statement: Assume AC. For $N\ge2$, $0<q<N$, and $R=\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb F_2$, the one-point compactification $(\mathbb R^N)^+$ of $\mathbb R^N$ ([[def-one-point-compactification]]) is homeomorphic to $S^N$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]) and has $H^q((\mathbb R^N)^+;R)=0$ ([[thm-topological-universal-coefficient-short-exact-sequence-for-cohomology]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).
entry.strategy:
1.1 Define $h:(\mathbb R^N)^{*}\to S^N$ by $$h(x)=\Big(\tfrac{2x}{1+\|x\|_2^2},\ \tfrac{\|x\|_2^2-1}{\|x\|_2^2+1}\Big),\qquad h(\infty)=(0,\dots,0,1),$$ writing $\|x\|_2^2$ for the squared Euclidean norm. For $x\in\mathbb R^N$ the identity $(2\|x\|_2)^2+(\|x\|_2^2-1)^2=(\|x\|_2^2+1)^2$ shows $\|h(x)\|_2=1$, so $h(x)\in S^N$; and $h(x)\neq(0,\dots,0,1)$ since $\|x\|_2^2-1=\|x\|_2^2+1$ is impossible. For $y=(y_1,\dots,y_{N+1})\in S^N$ with $y_{N+1}\neq1$ put $\psi(y):=(y_1,\dots,y_N)/(1-y_{N+1})\in\mathbb R^N$. If $r=\|\psi(y)\|_2$ then $r^2=(1-y_{N+1}^2)/(1-y_{N+1})^2=(1+y_{N+1})/(1-y_{N+1})$, so $1+r^2=2/(1-y_{N+1})$ and $r^2-1=2y_{N+1}/(1-y_{N+1})$; hence $h(\psi(y))=y$. Conversely, if $h(x)=(z,x_{N+1})$ then $1-x_{N+1}=2/(1+\|x\|_2^2)$ and $\psi(h(x))=2x/(1+\|x\|_2^2)\cdot(1+\|x\|_2^2)/2=x$. So $h$ is a bijection with inverse $\psi$ on $S^N\setminus\{(0,\dots,0,1)\}$ and $\infty\mapsto(0,\dots,0,1)$. [F3, algebra]

2.1 The map $h$ is continuous. On $\mathbb R^N$ its components $x\mapsto 2x_i/(1+\|x\|_2^2)$ and $x\mapsto(\|x\|_2^2-1)/(\|x\|_2^2+1)$ are quotients with denominator $1+\|x\|_2^2\ge1$ never zero, hence continuous by [F3]; the components are continuous, so $h|_{\mathbb R^N}$ is continuous into $\mathbb R^{N+1}$ and, since its image lies in $S^N$, continuous into the subspace $S^N$ by [F5]. At $\infty$, let $V\subseteq S^N$ be open with $(0,\dots,0,1)\in V$. The subspace topology on $S^N$ is the metric topology of the maximum metric, so there is $r>0$ such that every $y\in S^N$ with $\|y-(0,\dots,0,1)\|_\infty<r$ lies in $V$; choose $M\ge1$ with $1/M<r/2$ and put $C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^N:\|x\|_2\le M\}$, which is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F4]. For $x\notin C$ one has $\|x\|_2>M\ge1$, so $|2x_i/(1+\|x\|_2^2)|\le 2\|x\|_2/\|x\|_2^2=2/\|x\|_2<2/M<r$ and $|(\|x\|_2^2-1)/(\|x\|_2^2+1)-1|=2/(\|x\|_2^2+1)\le 2/\|x\|_2^2<2/M<r$; hence $h(x)\in V$. Therefore $W:=(\mathbb R^N)^{*}\setminus C$ is open in $(\mathbb R^N)^{*}$ by [F1], contains $\infty$, and satisfies $h(W)\subseteq V$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 Hence $h$ is a homeomorphism. Indeed $\mathbb R^N$ is locally compact and Hausdorff by [F2], so $(\mathbb R^N)^{*}$ is compact and Hausdorff by [F1], while $S^N$ is Hausdorff by [F2]; a continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism by [F5]. Consequently $h^{*}:H^q(S^N;R)\to H^q((\mathbb R^N)^{*};R)$ is an isomorphism for every $q$ by [F8]. [F1, F2, F5, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 By the homeomorphism of step 3.1 it suffices to compute $H^q(S^N;R)$. By [F7], $H_q(S^N;\mathbb Z)=0$ for $0<q<N$, while $H_0(S^N;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Apply the universal coefficient sequence of [F6] in degree $q$ with $X=S^N$ and $G=R$: $$0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(H_{q-1}(S^N;\mathbb Z),R)\longrightarrow H^q(S^N;R)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_q(S^N;\mathbb Z),R)\longrightarrow0.$$ If $q\ge2$ then $1\le q-1<q\le N-1$, so both $H_{q-1}$ and $H_q$ vanish and both outer terms are zero by [F7]. If $q=1$ (so $N\ge2$) then $H_1(S^N;\mathbb Z)=0$ and $H_0(S^N;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, so the right term is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(0,R)=0$ and the left term is $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z,R)=0$ by [F7]. In both cases exactness forces $H^q(S^N;R)=0$, for $R=\mathbb Z$ and for $R=\mathbb F_2$ alike. [F6, F7, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Combining steps 3.1 and 4.1, $H^q((\mathbb R^N)^{*};R)\cong H^q(S^N;R)=0$ for $0<q<N$, which is the claimed vanishing for the one-point compactification. The case $N=2$, $q=1$, both coefficient rings, and both orders of the two outer terms in the universal coefficient sequence are covered by the case distinction of step 4.1; the empty coefficient ring and negative $q$ are excluded by the hypotheses, and no further choice beyond AC, used through [F6] and [F7], enters. [F6, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

entry.title: An embedding into Euclidean space gives a rank-(n-m) stable normal inverse
entry.statement:
Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $i:M^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^n$ be a smooth embedding of a closed smooth $m$-manifold with $n>m$, and let $
u_i=i^*T\mathbb R^n/di(TM)$ be its normal quotient, identified with the orthogonal complement of $di(TM)$ by a Euclidean metric ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]], [[prop-an-ambient-riemannian-metric-identifies-the-normal-quotient-with-the-orthogonal-normal-bundle]]). Then $
u_i$ is a smooth real bundle of rank $n-m$, and the orthogonal splitting together with the canonical trivialization $i^*T\mathbb R^n\cong\varepsilon^n$ gives a smooth bundle isomorphism $\varphi:TM\oplus
u_i	o\varepsilon^n$. Hence $(
u_i,\varphi)$ is a rank-$(n-m)$ stable normal inverse of $M$ in the sense of [[def-stable-normal-inverse-of-the-tangent-bundle]]. Consequently every closed smooth $m$-manifold admits a stable normal inverse: apply [[thm-every-smooth-manifold-embeds-in-some-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]] to obtain an embedding into some $\mathbb R^N$. The countable-choice hypothesis is exactly the one inherited from the metric and tubular identifications of the published embedding normal-bundle definition; no further choice is made.
entry.strategy:
1.1 Regard $i$ as an embedding of $M$ as an embedded submanifold $i(M)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and let $\nu_i$ be its normal quotient as in [F1]. By [F3] the quotient carries a smooth real vector-bundle structure of rank $n-m$; the rank is the difference of the ranks of the ambient tangent bundle of $\mathbb R^n$ and of $di(TM)$, computed fibrewise, and equals $n-m$ because $di$ is fibrewise injective. [F1, F3, F6]

1.2 By [F2] the Euclidean metric identifies the quotient $\nu_i$ with the orthogonal complement $di(TM)^\perp$, which is a smooth subbundle of $i^*T\mathbb R^n$; the orthogonal decomposition of the Euclidean bundle gives $i^*T\mathbb R^n=di(TM)\oplus di(TM)^\perp\cong TM\oplus\nu_i$, where the first summand is identified with $TM$ through the isomorphism $di:TM\to di(TM)$. Composing this isomorphism with the canonical trivialization $i^*T\mathbb R^n\cong\varepsilon^n$ of [F4], which exists because the identity chart of $\mathbb R^n$ trivializes $T\mathbb R^n$ and the product-pullback lemma trivializes its pullback, gives a smooth bundle isomorphism $$\varphi:TM\oplus\nu_i\longrightarrow\varepsilon^n.$$ [F2, F3, F4]

2.1 Since $\nu_i$ has rank $n-m$ by step 1.1 and $\varphi$ is a smooth bundle isomorphism onto $\varepsilon^{n}=\varepsilon^{m+(n-m)}$, the pair $(\nu_i,\varphi)$ is a rank-$(n-m)$ stable normal inverse of $M$ in the sense of [F6]. [F2, F4, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 For existence, let $M$ be any closed smooth $m$-manifold. By [F5] there is a smooth embedding $j:M\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$ into some finite-dimensional Euclidean space; the construction above applies to $j$ provided $N>m$. If $N\le m$ for the particular embedding produced, compose with the inclusion $\mathbb R^N\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{N+1}\hookrightarrow\cdots\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{m+1}$ (each an embedding of a linear subspace as a closed subset, hence a smooth embedding with $di$ injective) to obtain an embedding into some $\mathbb R^n$ with $n>m$; replacing the ambient metric by the standard Euclidean one leaves the argument unchanged. Applying steps 1.1–2.1 to that embedding produces a stable normal inverse of $M$. The only choice principle used is the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ inherited from [F2] and [F5]; the trivialization [F4] is canonical, and no embedding, metric or complement is selected beyond the given ones. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

entry.title: An immersion into R^n gives a rank-(n-m) representative of the stable normal bundle
entry.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f:M^m\looparrowright\mathbb R^n$ be a smooth immersion of a closed smooth $m$-manifold with $n>m$, so that $(f,df)$ is a formal immersion and $
u_f=f^*T\mathbb R^n/df(TM)$ is its normal bundle of rank $n-m$ ([[def-formal-immersion-between-smooth-manifolds]], [[def-normal-bundle-of-a-formal-immersion]]). Then the splitting of the tangent-normal sequence of [[lem-formal-immersion-gives-the-tangent-normal-bundle-identity]] gives a smooth bundle isomorphism $TM\oplus
u_f	o f^*T\mathbb R^n$, which under the canonical trivialization $f^*T\mathbb R^n\cong\varepsilon^n$ becomes a smooth isomorphism $\varphi:TM\oplus
u_f	o\varepsilon^n$. Hence $(
u_f,\varphi)$ is a rank-$(n-m)$ stable normal inverse of $M$ in the sense of [[def-stable-normal-inverse-of-the-tangent-bundle]]: an immersion of codimension $n-m$ supplies an actual rank-$(n-m)$ representative of the inverse normal class, not merely a stable one. The choice hypothesis is inherited from the bundle-metric splitting in the normal-bundle construction.
entry.strategy:
1.1 Since $f$ is an immersion, $(f,df)$ is a formal immersion from $M^m$ to $\mathbb R^n$ by [F1]; in particular $df:TM	o f^*T\mathbb R^n$ is fibrewise injective. By [F2] its normal bundle $
u_f=f^*T\mathbb R^n/df(TM)$ is a smooth real vector bundle over $M$ of rank $n-m$. [F1, F2]

1.2 By [F3] the quotient sequence $0	o TM\xrightarrow{df}f^*T\mathbb R^n	o
u_f	o0$ splits: the tangent-normal sequence admits a smooth bundle isomorphism $$s:TM\oplus
u_f\longrightarrow f^*T\mathbb R^n$$ restricting to $df$ on the tangent summand. The splitting uses a smooth bundle metric on the pullback bundle (whose existence is the countable-choice input of that lemma), so this step uses exactly the hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and no more. [F2, F3]

2.1 Compose the splitting $s$ with the canonical trivialization $t:f^*T\mathbb R^n	o\varepsilon^n$ supplied by [F4], which exists because the identity chart of $\mathbb R^n$ trivializes $T\mathbb R^n$ and the product-pullback lemma trivializes its pullback along $f$: $$\varphi:=t\circ s:TM\oplus
u_f\longrightarrow\varepsilon^n$$ is a smooth bundle isomorphism, the composite of two smooth bundle isomorphisms. [F3, F4, step 1.2]

3.1 By step 1.1 the bundle $
u_f$ has rank $n-m$ and by step 2.1 the isomorphism $\varphi$ maps $TM\oplus
u_f$ onto $\varepsilon^{n}=\varepsilon^{m+(n-m)}$; so $(
u_f,\varphi)$ is a rank-$(n-m)$ stable normal inverse of $M$ in the sense of [F5]. Thus an immersion of codimension $n-m$ provides an actual rank-$(n-m)$ inverse bundle, not merely a stable one; nothing beyond this rank and the isomorphism is asserted about $
u_f$. The countable-choice hypothesis is the one inherited from the metric splitting of [F3] and from the canonical trivialization [F4]; no bundle metric, complement or frame is chosen in addition to those data. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

entry.title: Smale-Hirsch makes rank reduction sufficient for Euclidean immersion in positive codimension
entry.statement: Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M^m$ be a closed smooth $m$-manifold, let $k\ge1$, and let $(\nu,\varphi)$ be a rank-$k$ stable normal inverse of $M$, so that $\varphi:TM\oplus\nu\to\varepsilon^{m+k}$ ([[def-stable-normal-inverse-of-the-tangent-bundle]]). Then there exists an immersion $M\looparrowright\mathbb R^{m+k}$. Together with [[lem-an-immersion-into-r-n-gives-a-rank-n-minus-m-representative-of-the-stable-normal-bundle]] this says that for closed $M$ and $k\ge1$ the existence of an immersion $M\looparrowright\mathbb R^{m+k}$ is equivalent to the existence of a rank-$k$ stable normal inverse; that equivalence is the precise sense in which the normal problem is complete for immersions on this page. No classification of regular homotopy classes and no statement about the normal bundle of the particular immersion produced is asserted.
entry.strategy:
1.1 Define $F:=\varphi|_{TM}:TM\to\varepsilon^{m+k}$ as the restriction of the bundle isomorphism $\varphi$ to the first summand; this is a smooth bundle map over $M$, injective on every fibre. By [F4], it determines a smooth fibrewise injective map $TM\to c^*T\mathbb R^{m+k}$ over $\operatorname{id}_M$. Composing with the canonical map $c^*T\mathbb R^{m+k}\to T\mathbb R^{m+k}$ gives a smooth bundle map $\widetilde F$ over $c$, so $(c,\widetilde F)$ is a formal immersion by [F1]. Thus $\operatorname{FImm}(M,\mathbb R^{m+k})$ is nonempty. [F1, F4]

2.1 By [F2] with $N=\mathbb R^{m+k}$ (boundaryless, positive codimension $k\ge1$) the derivative map $D$ is a weak homotopy equivalence; by [F3] it induces a bijection on path components. Since $\operatorname{FImm}(M,\mathbb R^{m+k})$ is nonempty by step 1.1 and $\pi_0(D)$ is surjective, the target's empty-or-non-empty status matches the source's, so $\operatorname{Imm}(M,\mathbb R^{m+k})$ is nonempty: there exists a smooth immersion $M\looparrowright\mathbb R^{m+k}$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Conversely, every smooth immersion $M\looparrowright\mathbb R^{m+k}$ of the closed $M$ has a rank-$k$ normal bundle which is a rank-$k$ stable normal inverse by [F5], under the same $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Therefore for closed $M$ and $k\ge1$ the existence of an immersion into $\mathbb R^{m+k}$ is equivalent to the existence of a rank-$k$ stable normal inverse: reduction of the structure problem to the normal bundle is sufficient as well as necessary, which is the completeness statement of the design. The argument selects no immersion canonically (it only proves nonemptiness of a space), asserts nothing about the regular homotopy class of the immersion produced, and makes no claim about its normal bundle; the only choice used is the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ assumed by the Smale-Hirsch theorem and by the normal-bundle splitting. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

entry.title: The normal Stiefel-Whitney class is the multiplicative inverse of the tangent class
entry.statement:
Assume AC. Let $M$ be a closed smooth $m$-manifold, let $(
u,\varphi)$ be a stable normal inverse of $M$ with $\varphi:TM\oplus
u	o\varepsilon^N$, and let $w(E)=\sum_iw_i(E)$ denote the total Stiefel-Whitney class in the ring $H^*(M;\mathbb F_2)$ ([[def-stiefel-whitney-classes-from-the-projective-bundle-relation]], [[def-singular-cohomology-ring]]). Then $$w(TM)\,w(
u)=1\qquad	ext{in }H^*(M;\mathbb F_2).$$ Hence $w(
u)$ is the unique two-sided inverse of $w(TM)$, and the classes $w_i(
u)$ depend only on $M$, not on the chosen stable normal inverse $(
u,\varphi)$. Equivalently the total normal class is $w(
u)=w(TM)^{-1}=: ar w(M)$, the Whitney-duality form of the normal Stiefel-Whitney class.
entry.strategy:
1.1 By [F3] the isomorphism $\varphi$ gives $w(TM\oplus
u)=w(\varepsilon^N)$; by [F2], $w(TM\oplus
u)=w(TM)w(
u)$ and $w(\varepsilon^N)=1$, the latter because $\varepsilon^N$ is trivial and adjoining trivial summands does not change the classes. Hence $$w(TM)w(
u)=1\qquad	ext{in }H^*(M;\mathbb F_2).$$ The computation happens in the unital ring of [F5], and the bundles involved are numerable over the closed smooth manifold $M$ by [F4], so the cited Whitney and naturality theorems apply. [F2, F3, F4, F5]

2.1 Equation $w(TM)w(
u)=1$ exhibits $w(
u)$ as a two-sided inverse of $w(TM)$, and by [F5] the inverse of a unit is unique; in particular if $(
u_0,\varphi_0)$ and $(
u_1,\varphi_1)$ are two stable normal inverses then $w(
u_0)=w(TM)^{-1}=w(
u_1)$, so each $w_i(
u)$ depends only on $M$. This justifies the notation $ ar w(M):=w(TM)^{-1}=w(
u)$. The argument uses no property of $\varphi$ beyond its being a bundle isomorphism, no orientation of $M$, and only the choice assumed in AC, inherited through the AT suppliers [F1]–[F3]. [F2, F5, step 1.1] ∎

entry.title: The normal Pontryagin class is the rational inverse of the tangent Pontryagin class
entry.statement:
Assume AC. Let $M$ be a closed connected smooth $m$-manifold, let $(
u,\varphi)$ be a stable normal inverse of $M$ with $\varphi:TM\oplus
u	o\varepsilon^N$, and let $p(E)=\sum_ip_i(E)$ denote the total Pontryagin class in the AT normalization $p_i(E)=(-1)^ic_{2i}(E_{\mathbb C})$ ([[def-pontryagin-classes-by-complexification]]). Then $$p(TM)\,p(
u)=1\qquad	ext{in }H^*(M;\mathbb Q).$$ Hence $p(
u)$ is the unique inverse of $p(TM)$ in $H^*(M;\mathbb Q)$, and the classes $p_i(
u)$ depend only on $M$, not on the chosen stable normal inverse. All assertions in this item are over $\mathbb Q$. The integral Pontryagin Whitney product holds only modulo elements of order two, so no integral multiplicativity is asserted here. Orientation of $M$ is not needed, since $p_i$ is defined for every real bundle by complexification; connectedness is exactly the hypothesis of the AT Whitney-product item.
entry.strategy:
1.1 If $M$ is empty, its cohomology is the zero ring and the identity and inverse assertions hold with $0=1$. Otherwise choose a CW complex $K$ and maps $a:M	o K$, $b:K	o M$ with $ba\simeq\operatorname{id}_M$ by [F4]. The compact image $a(M)$ lies in a finite subcomplex; take its connected component $L$ containing $a(M)$, and restrict $b$ to $L$. A finite CW complex is compact Hausdorff (it is a finite union of characteristic-disk images), hence paracompact (every open cover has a finite, thus locally finite, subcover); its connected components are path connected. For each bundle $E$ among $TM,
u,TM\oplus
u,\varepsilon^N$, put $E_L=b^*E$. Pullback numerations make these bundles numerable. Then $a^*E_L\cong E$ by homotopy invariance, and Chern naturality in [F4] gives $p_i(E)=a^*p_i(E_L)$. Pullback preserves sums and trivial bundles in their charts. Thus the Whitney identity and stability of [F2] and [F3], applied on $L$ and pulled back along $a$, hold for the given bundles on $M$. Finally $\varphi$ gives $p(TM\oplus
u)=p(\varepsilon^N)$ by isomorphism invariance [F1]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 Over $\mathbb Q$, where $2$ is invertible, [F2] gives $p(TM\oplus
u)=p(TM)p(
u)$ in $H^*(M;\mathbb Q)$. For the trivial bundle, apply the stability clause of [F3] with the rank-zero bundle $0_M$: $p_i(\varepsilon^N)=p_i(0_M\oplus\varepsilon^N)=p_i(0_M)$ for every $i$, and the rank convention $p_i(0_M)=0$ for $i\ge1$ together with $p_0=1$ gives $p(\varepsilon^N)=1$. Combining with step 1.1, $$p(TM)p(
u)=p(TM\oplus
u)=p(\varepsilon^N)=1\qquad	ext{in }H^*(M;\mathbb Q).$$ [F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F5] the inverse of the unit $p(TM)$ in the unital ring $H^*(M;\mathbb Q)$ is unique, so $p(
u)=p(TM)^{-1}$ and the classes $p_i(
u)$ do not depend on the chosen stable normal inverse $(
u,\varphi)$. This is the rational form of the Pontryagin normal-class identity; no integral multiplicativity is obtained, because [F2] carries the two-torsion caveat and the odd Chern cross terms of a complexified real bundle can be nonzero two-torsion by [F1]. For a disconnected closed $M$ the same computation applies to each component, and the identity then holds componentwise. AC is inherited through [F2] and [F3]; no orientation of $M$ is used anywhere. [F1, F2, F5, step 2.1] ∎

entry.title: Normal Stiefel-Whitney and Pontryagin classes of a closed manifold
entry.statement:
Assume AC. Let $M$ be a closed smooth $m$-manifold and choose a stable normal inverse $(
u,\varphi)$ of $M$, which exists by [[lem-an-embedding-into-r-n-gives-the-same-normal-bundle-identity]] ($\mathrm{AC}$ implies the required countable choice by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], and the embedding lemma applies to closed $M$). Define the **total normal Stiefel-Whitney class** and the **total normal Pontryagin class** by $$ ar w(M):=w(
u)\in H^*(M;\mathbb F_2),\qquad  ar p(M):=p(
u)\in H^*(M;\mathbb Q),$$ with components $ ar w_i(M)\in H^i(M;\mathbb F_2)$ and $ ar p_i(M)\in H^{4i}(M;\mathbb Q)$ ([[def-stiefel-whitney-classes-from-the-projective-bundle-relation]], [[def-pontryagin-classes-by-complexification]], [[def-singular-cohomology-ring]]). By [[lem-normal-stiefel-whitney-class-is-the-multiplicative-inverse-of-the-tangent-class]] and [[lem-normal-pontryagin-class-is-the-rational-inverse-of-the-tangent-pontryagin-class]] the classes $ ar w_i(M)$ and, for connected $M$, the classes $ ar p_i(M)$ are independent of the chosen inverse, so the definition is well posed; equivalently $ ar w(M)=w(TM)^{-1}$ and $ ar p(M)=p(TM)^{-1}$ are the explicit inverses realized by any inverse bundle. For a disconnected closed $M$ the Pontryagin definition is applied componentwise. These are the classes also called the normal, dual, or (in Skopenkov's terminology) Stiefel-Whitney and Pontryagin classes of the manifold; they are the classes read by the immersion and embedding tests of this page.
entry.strategy: Definition of notation, with its local justification deferred to the two immediately preceding inverse lemmas, which prove that the choice of stable normal inverse does not affect the classes. Existence of an inverse is the embedding lemma with the Whitney embedding theorem. No choice beyond the suppliers' is used; the Pontryagin classes are entirely rational by the preceding lemma. The notation $\bar w_i$, $\bar p_i$ matches the design's $\bar w(T\mathbb RP^m)$ and the normal classes of the sources. AC implies the required countable-choice premise by [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]].
